708.title: The opening of the chest
708.hook: Muslim reports that as a boy his chest was opened by angels and his heart washed
708.howItsDone: Muslims know this event as sharh al-sadr, the opening of the chest; it is retold in sirah and hadith study, and some connect it with the opening of surah al-Sharh (94).

segments.voice: Yesterday, Halimah's thin donkey. Your line was: blessing came with him. Whose arrival did you name, and did you tell them? Day seven hundred eight.

Boys are playing in the open country of the Banu Sa'd. Suddenly they scatter and run, shouting to the boy's foster mother: Muhammad has been killed! The family rushes out and finds him alive, his face pale. Something has happened to him that the other children saw only from a distance. Sahih Muslim keeps the account, from Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ. Today: the opening of the chest.
screen: `BOYS AT PLAY.` → `"MUHAMMAD HAS BEEN KILLED!"` → `ALIVE, AND PALE.`

segments.voice: Here is what Muslim reports. While the boy was playing, Jibril came to him, laid him down, and opened his chest. He took out the heart, and from it drew out a clot, and said: this was the share of Satan in you. Then he washed the heart in a basin of gold, with the water of Zamzam, the well his grandfather found again, and put it back in its place. Anas adds a small detail that brings the whole thing close: he says he used to see the mark of the stitching on the Prophet's chest. Ibn Ishaq tells the same event in Halimah's voice, with two men in white, and says it frightened the family into taking the boy back to his mother in Mecca. So the sources differ on the details, and say so. What does the story mean? Readers take it in different ways. Some take it as a real event that happened to his body. Others stress what it points to: a heart prepared early, cleaned of what pulls toward harm, before anything was asked of it. Some commentators connect it with the opening of surah ninety-four, which Pickthall translates: "Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate." The Arabic there speaks of opening, or expanding, the chest. Notice what the story does not say. It doesn't say the boy did anything to earn it. He was playing. The washing came to him, the way water comes to a dry field. And notice the water: not something exotic, but Zamzam, the well from a few days ago, the water of Hajar's search.
screen: `JIBRIL OPENS THE CHEST.` · `WASHED WITH ZAMZAM IN A GOLD BASIN.` · `ANAS SAW THE STITCHING MARK.` · `A HEART PREPARED EARLY.` · then, large: `HAVE WE NOT CAUSED THY BOSOM TO DILATE.`

segments.voice: The practice: wash your hands and face slowly. If there's water near you, go to it now. If not, do this in your mind, just as slowly. Let cool water run over your hands. Feel the wrists, the palms, the space between the fingers. Then cup the water and bring it to your face. Hold it there for a breath. Muslims wash before prayer in a set order; this is not that, just a slow washing. As the water goes, let one thing you've been carrying go with it. If you pray, you can ask Allah for a clean heart in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The opening of the chest. In Sahih Muslim, Jibril opens the boy's chest, draws out the share of Satan, and washes the heart with Zamzam. Today's word.
screen: `THE OPENING OF THE CHEST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a washed heart. Today, each time you wash your hands, let it be slow for one breath, and set down one grudge with the water. Day seven hundred eight.

709.title: Aminah at Abwa
709.hook: his mother dies on the road home from Yathrib when he is six
709.howItsDone: Muslims who hear of a death say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, from surah 2:156, and visiting graves to remember death follows the Prophet's ﷺ words in Sahih Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of the chest. Your line was: a washed heart. When you washed your hands slowly, what did you set down with the water? Day seven hundred nine.

A grown man stops at a grave and weeps, and the people with him weep too. Sahih Muslim keeps the scene. The man is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the grave belongs to his mother. He was a small boy the last time he saw her alive. It happened far from home, on a journey, in a place called Abwa, on the road between Yathrib and Mecca. Today: Aminah at Abwa.
screen: `A GRAVE BY THE ROAD.` → `A GROWN MAN WEEPS.` → `HIS MOTHER'S GRAVE.`

segments.voice: After the boy came back from Halimah's people, he lived with his mother, Aminah, in Mecca. The sirah says that when he was six, she took him north to Yathrib, the oasis town that would one day be called Medina, to visit relatives there. With them, the sirah says, went Umm Ayman, a woman of the household who helped care for him. On the way home, at Abwa, Aminah fell ill and died. She was buried there. And Umm Ayman brought the boy the rest of the way to Mecca without her. Sit with that road for a moment. His father, Abdullah, had died before he was born, the sirah says. He never saw his father's face. Now he has seen his mother's for the last time. That's the line for today: an orphan twice. Ibn Ishaq tells it in a few plain sentences, and doesn't dwell. It's the hadith from much later that shows how deep it went. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet visits his mother's grave and weeps, and he tells the people with him that he asked his Lord for permission to visit it, and permission was given. Then he says: visit graves, because they remind you of death. So the grief that began on a road at Abwa becomes, years later, a teaching about remembering. Notice who carried him home. Umm Ayman stays in the story, and Muslims remember her with honor. A loss, and right beside it, a woman who did not let go of his hand.
screen: `A JOURNEY NORTH TO YATHRIB.` · `ILLNESS AND DEATH AT ABWA.` · `UMM AYMAN BRINGS HIM HOME.` · `THE GROWN MAN AT THE GRAVE.` · then, large: `AN ORPHAN TWICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember a mother who died young. It may be your own mother, or a friend's, or someone you only heard about, or a woman in a story. Settle, and breathe. Bring her to mind, and the child she left behind. Hold them both, gently, without needing to fix anything. If this is too close today, remember Aminah instead, on the road at Abwa. At news of a death, Muslims say a line from surah two, which Pickthall renders: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." If you pray, you can say it now. If not, just keep her in mind. The bell holds the time.

710.title: The grandfather's rug
710.hook: Abd al-Muttalib lets the boy sit on his rug by the Ka'ba, where no one else sat
710.howItsDone: Muslims teach kindness to children and respect for elders together, often citing the hadith that whoever does not show mercy to the young and honor the old is not one of us.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aminah at Abwa. Your line was: an orphan twice. Who did you think of, and did you say their parent's name to them? Day seven hundred ten.

In the shade of the Ka'ba, a rug is spread on the ground. It belongs to one man, Abd al-Muttalib, the old chief who found Zamzam again. His grown sons sit around its edge, the sirah says, and not one of them sits on it. Then a small boy, an orphan who has just lost his mother, walks past the circle of men and sits down on it. Today: the grandfather's rug.
screen: `A RUG IN THE KA'BA'S SHADE.` → `THE SONS SIT AROUND IT.` → `A SMALL BOY SITS ON IT.`

segments.voice: The boy is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, newly back in Mecca without his mother. Ibn Ishaq tells this scene briefly. His uncles reach for him to pull him off, because the rug is their father's place, and nobody takes it. And Abd al-Muttalib stops them. Leave my son alone, he says, in the sirah's telling, and he speaks of a great future for the boy. Then he sits him beside him and strokes his back, pleased with whatever the boy does. That's the whole scene. It's small. But it holds a lot. First, a seat. In a tribal town, where you sit says who you are. The rug by the Ka'ba is honor, made visible. Second, a hand. The uncles' hands reach to move him; the grandfather's hand rests on his back. Third, a word: my son. Not my grandson, not my dead son's boy. The man who once vowed to sacrifice a son, and ransomed Abdullah with camels, now calls Abdullah's orphan his own. And fourth, a lesson that the Prophet would later put into words. In a hadith collected by al-Tirmidhi, he says that whoever does not show mercy to the young, and honor to the old, is not one of us. Both halves are on the rug that day. An old man honored by his sons, and a child given mercy by the old man. The sirah does not tell us what the boy felt. It only tells us where he sat.
screen: `THE UNCLES REACH TO MOVE HIM.` · `"LEAVE MY SON ALONE."` · `A HAND ON HIS BACK.` · `MERCY TO THE YOUNG, HONOR TO THE OLD.` · then, large: `A PLACE BESIDE THE ELDER.`

segments.voice: The practice: make room for a child. Settle, and breathe. Think of a child in your life: a son or daughter, a niece, a student, the kid next door. Where is there a rug in your life they're usually kept off? A conversation, a table, a project, a quiet hour that's yours. Picture yourself moving over and patting the place beside you. What would you let them do there? What would you say? If you pray, you can ask Allah for patience with the young. If not, simply picture the space you'd make, and the child sitting down in it. The bell holds the time.
The grandfather's rug. Abd al-Muttalib's place by the Ka'ba, where his sons would not sit, and where, the sirah says, he let the orphan boy sit beside him. Today's word.
Your line: a place beside the elder. Today, let a child into one grown-up space: ask their opinion at the table, or let them help with something you'd usually do alone. Day seven hundred ten.

711.title: Abu Talib's house
711.hook: his uncle, poor and with many children, raises him as his own
711.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Talib as the uncle who raised and protected the Prophet ﷺ, and care for orphans is taught from surah 93 and from the Prophet's own childhood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grandfather's rug. Your line was: a place beside the elder. Did a child get a seat somewhere new in your day? Day seven hundred eleven.

One more grave. The old man who spread his rug by the Ka'ba dies too, the sirah says, while the boy is still young. Before he goes, Abd al-Muttalib asks one of his sons to take the orphan in. He chooses Abu Talib, the full brother of the boy's father, Abdullah, born of the same mother. And Abu Talib's house is already crowded, and his purse is thin. Today: Abu Talib's house.
screen: `THE GRANDFATHER DIES.` → `HE ENTRUSTS THE BOY.` → `A CROWDED HOUSE, A THIN PURSE.`

segments.voice: The sirah describes Abu Talib as a man of little money and a full house. Taking the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in means one more mouth at a table that's already stretched. He takes him anyway, and the sirah remembers his love for the boy. Ibn Ishaq says Abu Talib kept the boy close, and would take him along where he went. Notice the shape of this. The boy has lost a father he never saw, a mother on the road, and now a grandfather. Each time, someone stands in the gap. Halimah, who took the baby nobody wanted. Umm Ayman, who carried him home from Abwa. Abd al-Muttalib, on the rug. Now an uncle who can't really afford it. The Qur'an later speaks to the Prophet about exactly this. In surah ninety-three it reminds him that he was an orphan who was sheltered, and then it draws the line from his past to his duty. Pickthall translates: "Therefore the orphan oppress not." What was done for him, he is to do for others. And the story comes full circle in his own life. Years later, Ibn Ishaq says, when hard times fell on Quraysh and Abu Talib's family was struggling, Muhammad went to his uncle al-Abbas and proposed that each of them take one of Abu Talib's sons to ease the load. Muhammad took Ali, and raised him in his own home. The boy who was given room became the man who made room. There was room, both times, because someone decided there would be.
screen: `LITTLE MONEY, A FULL HOUSE.` · `ABU TALIB KEPT HIM CLOSE.` · `"THE ORPHAN OPPRESS NOT."` · `LATER, HE TAKES IN ALI.` · then, large: `THERE WAS ROOM.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank someone who stretched to include you. Settle, and breathe. Who made room for you when it cost them something? A relative who took you in for a while, a teacher who stayed late, a friend who shared a small apartment, someone whose budget or patience was already thin. Let one person come clearly to mind. Remember the table, or the couch, or the car. Say thank you to them in your heart, plainly, as if they were sitting across from you. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them. If not, just let the thanks be full. The bell holds the time.
Abu Talib's house. The crowded, hard-up home of the Prophet's uncle, who took the orphan in after his grandfather died, and kept him close. Today's word.
Your line: there was room. Today, make room for one more somewhere: an extra plate, a seat in the car, ten minutes for someone who asks. Day seven hundred eleven.

712.title: The shepherd
712.hook: he tends sheep for pay, and later says every prophet was a shepherd (Bukhari)
712.howItsDone: Muslims quote the hadith 'each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock' when speaking of responsibility in families, work and leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Talib's house. Your line was: there was room. Where did you make room for one more? Day seven hundred twelve.

Arak berries, small and dark, picked off the bush by a group of men on the road. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is with them, a grown man now, and he tells them: pick the black ones, they're the best. Someone asks him a question about that. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the question, and his answer opens a door onto the hills outside Mecca and a young man with a stick and a flock. Today: the shepherd.
screen: `ARAK BERRIES BY THE ROAD.` → `"PICK THE BLACK ONES."` → `A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The companions ask: were you a shepherd? And in al-Bukhari's report he answers with a question of his own: is there any prophet who was not? In another report in al-Bukhari, he says it plainly. Allah sent no prophet who did not tend sheep. They ask: and you? Yes, he says. I tended them for the people of Mecca, for a few coins. So the orphan from Abu Talib's crowded house earned his keep in the hills, walking slowly behind other people's animals. The Qur'an knows this work. In surah twenty, Allah asks Musa what is in his right hand, and Musa answers, in Pickthall's words: "This is my staff whereon I lean, and wherewith I beat down branches for my sheep, and wherein I find other uses." A man about to be sent to Pharaoh, and his first answer is about sheep. Why would shepherding come before prophethood? The hadith doesn't explain, and it's fair to leave that open. Commentators have offered reasons: sheep are slow and they scatter, and a shepherd learns patience, watchfulness, and how to bring back the one that wanders. Whatever the reason, the Prophet carried the word into his teaching. In al-Bukhari he says: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. The ruler, the parent, the worker with someone else's property. In Arabic, a shepherd is ra'i, and the flock is ra'iyyah, from the same root. Everyone, in that saying, is watching over something.
screen: `"IS THERE A PROPHET WHO WAS NOT?"` · `FOR THE PEOPLE OF MECCA, FOR COINS.` · `MUSA'S STAFF, FOR HIS SHEEP.` · `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · then, large: `EVERY PROPHET WAS A SHEPHERD.`

segments.voice: The practice: care for something small and slow. Settle, and breathe. What's in your keeping that moves at its own pace? A plant, a pet, an old parent, a child learning to read, a project that won't be rushed. Bring it to mind, and match its speed. Don't hurry it in your head. Watch it the way a shepherd watches a flock, noticing which part is wandering off. What would bringing it back gently look like today? If you pray, you can ask Allah for a shepherd's patience. If not, just stay slow with it. The bell holds the time.
The shepherd. The Prophet tended sheep for the people of Mecca, and said in al-Bukhari that Allah sent no prophet who did not. Today's word.
Your line: every prophet was a shepherd. Today, give one slow thing in your care ten unhurried minutes: water it, walk it, sit with it, read with it. Day seven hundred twelve.

713.title: The monk at Bosra
713.hook: the sirah tells of a Christian monk, Bahira, who saw signs in the boy on a caravan to Syria
713.howItsDone: The story of Bahira is told in sirah books and classes about the Prophet's ﷺ youth, with some teachers noting which parts are well supported and which are weaker.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherd. Your line was: every prophet was a shepherd. What slow thing did you give your unhurried time to? Day seven hundred thirteen.

A stone cell by the trade road near Bosra, on the edge of Syria. Caravans from Mecca have passed it often, and the monk inside has never spoken to them, the sirah says. This time he does. He sends word to the travelers: I've prepared food, and I want every one of you to come, young and old, slave and free. The merchants of Quraysh look at each other. What's changed? Today: the monk at Bosra.
screen: `A MONK'S CELL BY THE ROAD.` → `HE NEVER SPOKE TO THEM BEFORE.` → `"EVERY ONE OF YOU, COME."`

segments.voice: The caravan belongs to Abu Talib, and he has brought his nephew, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, still a boy. Ibn Ishaq tells the story. The monk is named Bahira, a Christian who, the sirah says, had learned from a book kept in that cell. He has seen something from his window: a cloud shading one traveler as the caravan came in, and a tree bending its branches over him where he sat. At the meal, the boy isn't there. He's been left with the baggage, the youngest. Bahira insists: bring him. Then he watches him closely, and asks him questions. When Bahira asks in the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the idols of Mecca, the boy refuses to be asked by them. Bahira asks in God's name instead, and the boy answers. Finally the monk looks at his back and sees a mark between his shoulders. Bahira turns to Abu Talib with a warning: take your brother's son home, and guard him carefully. And Abu Talib does. How should this be heard? Carefully. Al-Tirmidhi records a version of the journey too, and some hadith scholars have questioned parts of it, so it's honest to hold the details lightly. What stays is the shape. On a dusty road, a stranger from another faith looked closely at an orphan boy left with the bags and saw something worth protecting. The sirah keeps this Christian monk in the story with respect, as a neighbor who recognized goodness when it walked in.
screen: `A CLOUD, A BENDING TREE.` · `"BRING THE BOY."` · `HE WON'T SWEAR BY THE IDOLS.` · `"TAKE HIM HOME AND GUARD HIM."` · then, large: `SOMEONE SAW IT EARLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice who recognizes goodness. Settle, and breathe. Think back to someone who saw something good in you before you saw it yourself. A teacher, a coach, a neighbor, an older cousin, a stranger even, who looked twice and said something that stayed. Let their face come back, and their words. Now turn it around. Is there someone near you, left with the bags, so to speak, whose goodness no one has named yet? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open your eyes to it. If not, just hold that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
The monk at Bosra. Bahira, a Christian monk on the road to Syria, who, the sirah says, saw signs in the boy and told Abu Talib to guard him. Today's word.
Your line: someone saw it early. Today, be that someone once: tell a person, especially a young one, one good thing you see in them that nobody has said out loud. Day seven hundred thirteen.

714.title: The league of the virtuous
714.hook: as a young man he joins a pact of Meccan clans to defend anyone wronged, which he later praised
714.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite the Hilf al-Fudul as an example of the Prophet ﷺ honoring a just pact made before Islam, and it is invoked in discussions of justice and of working with others for the common good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monk at Bosra. Your line was: someone saw it early. Whose overlooked goodness did you name out loud? Day seven hundred fourteen.

A trader from Yemen has sold his goods in Mecca to a powerful man, and the man won't pay. The stranger has no clan in the city, nobody to call on. So, later sirah books say, he climbs a hill near the Ka'ba and calls out his complaint in verse, loud enough for the gathered men of Quraysh to hear. It's a gamble: shouting into a town where belonging protects you, and he belongs to no one there. Today: the league of the virtuous.
screen: `A STRANGER, UNPAID.` → `NO CLAN TO CALL ON.` → `A CRY FROM THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Someone hears him. In Ibn Ishaq's account, several clans of Quraysh gather at the house of a man named Abdullah ibn Jud'an. There they make a pact. They swear that whenever anyone in Mecca is wronged, whether from the city or a stranger, they will stand together on that person's side until what was taken is returned. And the later books say they went straight to the man who wouldn't pay, and made him pay. The pact came to be called the Hilf al-Fudul: the league of the virtuous, or the league of the excellent. Among those present, the sirah says, was the young Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Hold that against what we've seen this week. In a town where your clan was your protection, here was a promise to protect people with no clan at all. The orphan from Abu Talib's house is standing in the room where it's made. And he didn't forget it. Years later, after the revelation, he spoke of that day. The sirah reports him saying he had witnessed a pact in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an that he would not trade for a herd of red camels, prize animals, and that if he were called to it even now, in Islam, he would answer. A promise made in the days before Islam, among men who still prayed to idols, and he says he'd keep it. Teachers draw a lesson from that: a just promise is worth keeping, whoever first made it. The Qur'an later commands believers to stand firm for justice, as witnesses for God, even against themselves or their kin. The young man in Ibn Jud'an's house had already seen what that looked like.
screen: `CLANS MEET AT IBN JUD'AN'S HOUSE.` · `AN OATH FOR ANYONE WRONGED.` · `HE WAS IN THE ROOM.` · `"I WOULD ANSWER IT EVEN NOW."` · then, large: `DEFEND THE WRONGED.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand with someone treated unfairly. Settle, and breathe. Who near you is the stranger on the hill right now? A coworker blamed for someone else's mistake, a neighbor being talked about, a new kid, a person owed something they can't collect. Let one name or face come. Now ask, quietly: what's one thing I could do that would put me on their side? Not a grand rescue. A word, a witness, a message, a seat beside them. Hold the step until it feels possible. If you pray, you can ask Allah for courage. The bell holds the time.
The league of the virtuous. Hilf al-Fudul, the pact of Meccan clans to stand with anyone wronged, which the Prophet witnessed as a young man and later said he would still answer. Today's word.
screen: `THE LEAGUE OF THE VIRTUOUS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: defend the wronged. Today, take the one step you held in the practice, even a small one, for the person being treated unfairly. Day seven hundred fourteen.

fork.setup: you're a stranger in Mecca. a powerful man has your goods and won't pay. you have no clan in the city. what do you do?
options: give up and go home.
call out your complaint from a hill by the Ka'ba.
steal back what you're owed.
fork.reveal: later sirah books say he cried out in verse; clans of Quraysh made a pact and got him his due.

original.note: Arabic: hilf, a pact or alliance; al-fudul, often rendered the virtuous or the excellent.

trapdoor: what you thought: a business dispute in old Mecca.
what it means: clans swore to stand with anyone wronged, and the Prophet kept faith with that promise.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's account at Ibn Jud'an's house, and the report that he'd answer it even in Islam.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Hilf al-Fudul at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an; 'I would not exchange it for red camels')
Later sirah tradition, e.g. Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (the unpaid trader from Yemen; his cry from the hill; the debtor made to pay)
Qur'an 4:135 (stand firm for justice, as witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves or your kin)
